problem: Imitation learning of continuous visuo-motor policies had worked for static manipulation and for navigation, but not for mobile manipulation (MM). Two things block it. First, no interface lets humans easily demonstrate simultaneous base and arm control from onboard views. Prior MM imitation-learning work relied on instrumented environments or privileged views and only parametrized action primitives. Second, policies trained on limited demonstrations suffer severe covariate shift in MM's huge state space.
motivation: MM agents can do many more household tasks than navigation-only or manipulation-only robots, but the joint state space makes RL exploration intractable. A state-of-the-art RL baseline (ReLMoGen) scores 0% on every task. Human demonstrations have removed the exploration burden in static manipulation, so the authors ask whether scalable teleoperation plus imitation learning can do the same for MM. Because demonstrations can never cover the MM state space, they also want the agent to recognize when it has drifted out of distribution and stop or reset.
key_idea: Collect large-scale MM demonstrations with a smartphone teleoperation interface (MoMaRT) and train a BC policy with a multi-timescale RNN. Pair the policy with a goal-conditioned cVAE whose reconstruction error flags out-of-distribution states, which triggers an arm-reset 'recover' action or episode termination.
insight: Demonstration quality matters most. Training on the same number of expert rather than novice demonstrations raises success by over 200% on average (e.g., Table Cleanup to Sink 61.1 vs 8.9 SR for BC-TieredRNN). Imitation learning with human data succeeds where shaped-reward RL (ReLMoGen) never gets past approaching the bowl. The multi-timescale TieredRNN helps only on tasks that need memory: randomized trash-bin location (Table Cleanup tasks) and searching drawers (Table Setup from Dresser). It is worse than BC-RNN on tasks without such randomization. For error detection, Table A.3 shows cVAE reconstruction error clearly beats KL divergence, VAE encoder variance and policy log-probability as the OOD signal; the latent and policy-uncertainty signals are noisy and do not transfer across tasks at a fixed threshold. Noisier suboptimal data yields high precision (>90%) but much lower recall, because it widens the modeled state distribution. Few-shot adaptation after rearranging furniture works better by finetuning from the expert model than by training from scratch (Table A.4).
method: MoMaRT teleoperation: extends RoboTurk. A smartphone's 6-DoF motion drives the arm end-effector while an on-screen hourglass joystick with a dead-zone drives the non-holonomic base simultaneously. Head pan is fixed and head tilt auto-tracks the end-effector. A one-button arm reset moves the arm to a stable default configuration. The operator sees only the robot's onboard camera, streamed over WebRTC.

Dataset: 5 long-horizon kitchen tasks in iGibson/PyBullet with a Fetch robot manipulating a bowl, with randomized robot pose, bowl location and trash can. Each task has >110 expert and >110 suboptimal demonstrations plus >20 few-shot demonstrations with the dishwasher, dresser and sink swapped. Total is >1200 demonstrations and >11 h.

BC-TieredRNN policy: behavioral cloning with a GMM action head (5 modes) on 50-step sequences. N stacked RNN tiers update at different periods (horizons [50,5], strides [1,10], hidden [1000,400], z-dim 32). Each higher tier passes its encoding z_i down to the next faster tier to carry long-range context. Inputs are head and wrist RGB-D plus the base laser scan.

Error detector: a conditional VAE with a GMM latent prior (10 modes, latent dim 16) encodes the current state and a goal state H steps ahead, then reconstructs the goal conditioned on the current state. At test time it is applied backward: s=s_{t-H}, s_g=s_t. A reconstruction error above ψ=0.05 flags an OOD state.

Intervention: the first detected error triggers 'recover', which resets the arm to a default pose. If the error persists after recovery, or K errors have occurred, 'terminate' ends the episode, e.g., to ask a human for help.

setting.backbone: BC-TieredRNN with GMM action head (conv/MLP encoders) + GMM-prior cVAE error detector, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: MoMaRT kitchen demonstrations, all teleoperated in simulation: >110 expert and >110 suboptimal (novice) successful demos per task, plus >20 few-shot demos per task with rearranged furniture. Total >1200 demos, >11 h, over 5 tasks. Models are trained per task for 30 epochs. Few-shot models are finetuned from the expert models.
setting.observation: head-camera RGB-D + wrist-camera RGB-D (90x120) + base laser scan point cloud (1x100); egocentric only
setting.action_space: continuous 10-D at 20 Hz: base differential-drive linear/angular velocity + 6-DoF normalized delta end-effector command (IK controller) + grasp + arm-reset
setting.simulator: iGibson (PyBullet), Fetch robot, single realistic kitchen

numbers_note: The paper evaluates only on its own 5 MoMaRT kitchen mobile-manipulation tasks (iGibson), not on standard navigation benchmarks. There are no official splits, so 'test' denotes evaluation rollouts in the training kitchen, with randomized robot pose, bowl location and trash can. All values are means; ± std omitted. The SR in Table 1 (average of top-3 best evaluations over 30 episodes x 3 seeds) and 'SR (no ED)' in Table 2 come from different evaluation runs of the same model family and differ noticeably (e.g., 47.8 vs 34.4). The few-shot 'SR' is from Table A.4 and differs from Table 2's SR (no ED). ReLMoGen training curves appear only in a figure; its Table 1 SR is 0.0 on all tasks.
results: Trained on expert demonstrations, BC-TieredRNN reaches 47.8 / 61.1 / 68.1 / 66.2 / 47.8% SR on the five tasks. It beats BC-RNN (44.4 / 54.4 / 64.8) on the three memory-dependent tasks but is worse on Table Setup from Dishwasher (66.2 vs 68.5) and Unload Dishwasher to Dresser (47.8 vs 56.0). RL with ReLMoGen scores 0% on every task. The cVAE reconstruction-error detector reaches 85.8–100% precision and 85.9–100% recall on expert data with small SR changes. It outperforms KL-divergence, encoder-variance and policy-log-probability detectors. Under the furniture-rearranged few-shot shift, finetuned policies drop to 11.5–26.3% SR, yet the detector keeps high precision/recall.
limitations: Simulation only (iGibson, one kitchen, one object type, the bowl); no real-robot deployment, and sim-to-real physics gaps are acknowledged.

The TieredRNN gain is marginal and task-dependent (worse than BC-RNN on 2 of 5 tasks). The 'recover' action is not expected to succeed reliably, and the error detector can lower SR noticeably, especially in the few-shot setting (e.g., 24.4 to 11.1 on Table Cleanup to Sink).

The detector threshold ψ is hand-set from a few expert rollouts. The teleoperation interface is hard to master: 50% of novice users achieved no success in 30 minutes, and suboptimal data sharply reduces policy SR.
